\begin{proof}
Let $x$ be the unique element of order $2$ in $G$. For arbitrary $y\in G$, define $z=y^{-1}xy$. We have
\[
z^2=y^{-1}x^2y=y^{-1}ey=e.
\]
Moreover, $z\neq e$, since otherwise $x=yey^{-1}=e$, contradicting that $x$ has order $2$. Thus $z$ has order $2$. By uniqueness, $z=x$, and therefore $y^{-1}xy=x$. Multiplying by $y$ on the left and right gives $xy=yx$. Since $y$ was arbitrary, $x$ lies in the center of $G$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}
Let $x$ denote the only element of order $2$ in $G$. Take any $g\in G$. The elements $x$ and $g^{-1}xg$ are conjugate, so they have the same order. Consequently, $g^{-1}xg$ also has order $2$. The uniqueness hypothesis therefore implies
\[
g^{-1}xg=x.
\]
Equivalently, $xg=gx$. Since this holds for every $g\in G$, $x\in Z(G)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}
Let $x$ be the unique element of order $2$ in $G$. For each $y\in G$, conjugation by $y$ is an automorphism, so it preserves element orders. Hence $y^{-1}xy$ has order $2$. By the uniqueness assumption,
\[
y^{-1}xy=x.
\]
Multiplying this equality on the left by $y$ and on the right by $y^{-1}$ yields $xy=yx$. This holds for every $y\in G$, so $x$ commutes with every element of $G$ and therefore $x\in Z(G)$.
\end{proof}
